subject: math
title: Patterns and Relationships: Two Rules, Ordered Pairs and Graphs
seo_title: Grade 5 Numerical Patterns Worksheets: Two Rules, Corresponding Terms, Ordered Pairs and Graphs (5.OA.B.3)
standard_text: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 0, and given the rule “Add 6” and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 numerical patterns worksheets: make two patterns from two rules, find the relationship between corresponding terms, form ordered pairs and graph them on a coordinate plane, plus word problems. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Compare terms in the same place. Add 3 and Add 6 from 0 give 3 and 6, 6 and 12, 9 and 18: B is always 2 times A.
key_sub: Why: every step B adds 6, which is 2 times 3, so B has always added twice as much. Write each pair as (A term, B term) and graph it: right by the A term, up by the B term.
body_html:
Two rules make two patterns

Each pattern has a start number and a rule. Write the start number first, then use the rule again and again. Put the two patterns in a table so the terms in the same place line up.

Term1st2nd3rd4th5th
Pattern A: start 0, Add 3036912
Pattern B: start 0, Add 606121824

Compare corresponding terms

Corresponding terms are in the same place: the 3rd term of A (6) and the 3rd term of B (12). Compare down each column: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 9 × 2 = 18. Each B term is 2 times the A term.

Why? Both patterns start at 0, and every step B adds 6 while A adds 3. 6 is 2 × 3, so B has always added 2 times as much as A.

Example

Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. A term of A is 20. What is the B term?

12 = 3 × 4, so each B term is 3 times the A term. 20 × 3 = 60.

Answer: 60

If both patterns add the same number but start at different numbers, the difference stays the same: start 0 and start 4, both Add 3, gives 0 and 4, 3 and 7, 6 and 10. B is always 4 more than A.

Make ordered pairs

Write each column as an ordered pair (A term, B term): (0, 0), (3, 6), (6, 12), (9, 18), (12, 24). The A term comes first.

Graph the ordered pairs

Example

Which ordered pair comes after (12, 24)?

A adds 3 and B adds 6: (12 + 3, 24 + 6).

Answer: (15, 30)

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Comparing only the first pair: 3 and 6, so “B is 3 more”Check every column: 6 and 12 are 6 apart, but B is always 2 times A
Mixing up the rule and the relationshipThe rule (Add 6) goes along a row. The relationship (2 times) goes down a column
Switching the order: (6, 3)Write (A term, B term): (3, 6)
Pairing terms from different places, like (6, 18)Pair the 3rd term with the 3rd term: (6, 12)
Counting grid spaces on a scaled axisRead the numbers on the axes

faq.a: It is the Common Core Grade 5 standard for making two number patterns from two rules, comparing the terms in the same place, writing them as ordered pairs and graphing them on a coordinate plane.
They are the terms in the same place in two patterns, such as the 4th term of Pattern A and the 4th term of Pattern B. With Add 3 and Add 6 from 0, the 4th terms are 9 and 18.

faq.q: Why is one pattern twice the other when the rules are Add 3 and Add 6?
faq.a: Both start at 0, and each step the second pattern adds 6, which is 2 times 3. So it has always added twice as much, and each term is 2 times the matching term.

faq.q: How do you graph two numerical patterns?
faq.a: Pair the terms in the same place as (first pattern term, second pattern term), then plot each pair: go right by the first number and up by the second.

sets.title: Make two patterns from two rules

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 6 each time. The term before the ? is 6, so 6 + 6 = 12. (Adding 3 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 8. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 8 each time. The term before the ? is 16, so 16 + 8 = 24. (Adding 2 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern A adds 4 each time. The term before the ? is 8, so 8 + 4 = 12. (Adding 12 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 10. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 10 each time. The term before the ? is 30, so 30 + 10 = 40. (Adding 5 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 7. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 7 each time. The term before the ? is 7, so 7 + 7 = 14. (Adding 1 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 2, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 5, Add 3. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 3 each time. The term before the ? is 11, so 11 + 3 = 14.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 10. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 30. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 30 each time. The term before the ? is 60, so 60 + 30 = 90. (Adding 10 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 250. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 500. What number goes in the ? box?
items.e: Pattern B adds 500 each time. The term before the ? is 1,500, so 1,500 + 500 = 2,000. (Adding 250 uses the rule of the other pattern.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 8. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern B?
items.e: Pattern B starts at 0, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 8 each time: 0, 8, 16, 24, 32.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 15. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern B?
items.e: Pattern B starts at 0, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 15 each time: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 6. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern A?
items.e: Pattern A starts at 0, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 6 each time: 0, 6, 12, 18, 24.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 3, Add 4. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern B?
items.e: Pattern B starts at 3, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 4 each time: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 40. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 120. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern B?
items.e: Pattern B starts at 0, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 120 each time: 0, 120, 240, 360, 480.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 1, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 4, Add 2. Which list shows the first five terms of Pattern A?
items.e: Pattern A starts at 1, and the start is the 1st term. Then add 2 each time: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. What is the 6th term of Pattern B?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 6th term there are 5 jumps, not 6. 0 + 5 × 12 = 60.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 9. What is the 8th term of Pattern B?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 8th term there are 7 jumps, not 8. 0 + 7 × 9 = 63.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 5, Add 4. What is the 7th term of Pattern B?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 7th term there are 6 jumps, not 7. 5 + 6 × 4 = 29.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 50. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 150. What is the 10th term of Pattern B?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 10th term there are 9 jumps, not 10. 0 + 9 × 150 = 1,350.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 6. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 18. What is the 9th term of Pattern A?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 9th term there are 8 jumps, not 9. 0 + 8 × 6 = 48.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 25. What is the 12th term of Pattern B?
items.e: From the 1st term to the 12th term there are 11 jumps, not 12. 0 + 11 × 25 = 275.

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 3 × 2 = 6, 6 × 2 = 12, 9 × 2 = 18. Each B term is 2 times the A term. (“B is 3 more than A” works only for 3 and 6: 12 is 6 more than 6.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 2 × 4 = 8, 4 × 4 = 16, 6 × 4 = 24. Each B term is 4 times the A term. (“B is 6 more than A” works only for 2 and 8: 16 is 12 more than 4.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 5 × 3 = 15, 10 × 3 = 30, 15 × 3 = 45. Each B term is 3 times the A term. (“B is 10 more than A” works only for 5 and 15: 30 is 20 more than 10.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 4 × 5 = 20, 8 × 5 = 40, 12 × 5 = 60. Each B term is 5 times the A term. (“B is 16 more than A” works only for 4 and 20: 40 is 32 more than 8.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 6 × 2 = 12, 12 × 2 = 24, 18 × 2 = 36. Each B term is 2 times the A term. (“B is 6 more than A” works only for 6 and 12: 24 is 12 more than 12.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 7 × 3 = 21, 14 × 3 = 42, 21 × 3 = 63. Each B term is 3 times the A term. (“B is 14 more than A” works only for 7 and 21: 42 is 28 more than 14.)

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 0 + 4 = 4, 3 + 4 = 7, 6 + 4 = 10. Each B term is 4 more than the A term. The rule Add 3 tells how each pattern grows, not how A and B compare.

items.q: Compare each B term with the A term in the same column. Which is true for every pair of corresponding terms?
items.e: Look down each column: 1 + 6 = 7, 6 + 6 = 12, 11 + 6 = 17. Each B term is 6 more than the A term. The rule Add 5 tells how each pattern grows, not how A and B compare.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. Why is each B term 2 times the A term?
c: B starts at a bigger number
B always adds 3 more than A
items.e: Both patterns start at 0. Each step, B adds 6 and A adds 3, and 6 = 2 × 3. After any number of steps, B has added 2 times as much as A, so B is 2 times A: for example 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 6 = 24.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 4, Add 5. Why is each B term always 4 more than the A term?
c: Both add 5, and B starts 4 higher
items.e: B starts 4 higher (4 − 0 = 4). Each step both patterns add the same number, 5, so the difference never changes: 0 and 4, 5 and 9, 10 and 14.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. Will the 100th term of B still be 3 times the 100th term of A?
c: Yes, both use the same number of jumps
No, it works only for small terms
items.e: The 100th term of each pattern comes after 99 jumps. A is 99 × 4 and B is 99 × 12 = 99 × 3 × 4. B is 3 times A for every term, however far you go.

items.q: Pattern A: 0, 5, 10, 15. Pattern B: 0, 20, 40, 60. Owen says, “B is 15 more than A.” What mistake did he make?
c: He used the wrong rule for A
items.e: 20 is 15 more than 5, but 40 is 30 more than 10. Check every pair: 5 × 4 = 20, 10 × 4 = 40, 15 × 4 = 60. B is 4 times A.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. A term in Pattern A is 27. What is the corresponding term in Pattern B?
items.e: 12 = 4 × 3 and both start at 0, so each B term is 4 times the A term: 27 × 4 = 108. (Adding 4 or adding 12 to 27 does not use the relationship.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 10. A term in Pattern B is 60. What is the corresponding term in Pattern A?
items.e: Each B term is 5 times the A term (10 = 5 × 2). Work backward: 60 ÷ 5 = 12. Check: 12 × 5 = 60. (300 = 60 × 5 goes the wrong way.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 6, Add 5. A term in Pattern A is 45. What is the corresponding term in Pattern B?
items.e: Both patterns add 5, and B starts 6 higher, so each B term is 6 more than the A term: 45 + 6 = 51. (45 × 6 = 270 treats it as times.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 250. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 750. A term in Pattern A is 1,500. What is the corresponding term in Pattern B?
items.e: 750 = 3 × 250, so each B term is 3 times the A term: 1,500 × 3 = 4,500. (1,500 + 750 = 2,250 is just one more jump of B's rule.)

items.q: Each term in Pattern B is 6 times the corresponding term in Pattern A. The 5th term of Pattern A is 32. What is the 5th term of Pattern B?
items.e: Corresponding terms are in the same place: the 5th term with the 5th term. 32 × 6 = 192. (32 + 6 = 38 adds instead of multiplying, and 32 × 5 uses the term number.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 9. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 18. A term in Pattern B is 126. What is the corresponding term in Pattern A?
items.e: Each B term is 2 times the A term (18 = 2 × 9). So A is half of B: 126 ÷ 2 = 63. Check: 63 × 2 = 126.

items.q: Pattern A: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. Pattern B: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60. What is the rule for Pattern B?
items.e: A rule tells how to get the next term in the same pattern: 0 + 15 = 15, 15 + 15 = 30. “B is 3 times A” is the relationship between the two patterns, not B's rule.

items.q: Pattern A: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. Pattern B: 0, 15, 30, 45, 60. Which describes the relationship between corresponding terms?
items.e: Compare terms in the same place: 5 and 15, 10 and 30, 15 and 45. Each B term is 3 times the A term. Add 15 is only B's rule.

sets.title: Form ordered pairs from corresponding terms

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 6 is the 3rd term of A and 12 is the 3rd term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (6, 12). (12, 6) has the numbers switched.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 6 is the 4th term of A and 30 is the 4th term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (6, 30). (30, 6) has the numbers switched.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 4 is the 2nd term of A and 12 is the 2nd term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (4, 12). (12, 4) has the numbers switched.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 15 is the 4th term of A and 60 is the 4th term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (15, 60). (60, 15) has the numbers switched.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 5 is the 3rd term of A and 8 is the 3rd term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (5, 8). (8, 5) has the numbers switched.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (A term, B term). Which ordered pair is made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 200 is the 3rd term of A and 600 is the 3rd term of B, so they correspond. Write the A term first: (200, 600). (600, 200) has the numbers switched.

items.q: These ordered pairs come from two patterns: (0, 0), (2, 6), (4, 12), (6, 18), ? Which ordered pair comes next?
items.e: The first numbers go up by 2 and the second numbers go up by 6. After (6, 18) comes (6 + 2, 18 + 6) = (8, 24).

items.q: These ordered pairs come from two patterns: (0, 0), (4, 8), (8, 16), (12, 24), ? Which ordered pair comes next?
items.e: The first numbers go up by 4 and the second numbers go up by 8. After (12, 24) comes (12 + 4, 24 + 8) = (16, 32).

items.q: These ordered pairs come from two patterns: (0, 0), (5, 20), (10, 40), (15, 60), ? Which ordered pair comes next?
items.e: The first numbers go up by 5 and the second numbers go up by 20. After (15, 60) comes (15 + 5, 60 + 20) = (20, 80).

items.q: These ordered pairs come from two patterns: (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), ? Which ordered pair comes next?
items.e: The first numbers go up by 1 and the second numbers go up by 3. After (3, 9) comes (3 + 1, 9 + 3) = (4, 12).

items.q: These ordered pairs come from two patterns: (0, 0), (25, 75), (50, 150), (75, 225), ? Which ordered pair comes next?
items.e: The first numbers go up by 25 and the second numbers go up by 75. After (75, 225) comes (75 + 25, 225 + 75) = (100, 300).

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. Which ordered pair (A term, B term) is not made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 6 is in A and 24 is in B, so the pair must be written (6, 24). (24, 6) has the numbers switched. The other pairs all have B = 4 × A.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 10. Which ordered pair (A term, B term) is not made from corresponding terms?
items.e: 6 is the 4th term of A, but 40 is the 5th term of B. The 4th term of B is 30, so the pair should be (6, 30). In every correct pair, B is 5 times A.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 2, Add 5. Which ordered pair (A term, B term) is not made from corresponding terms?
items.e: Each B term is 2 more than the A term, so the pair for 15 is (15, 17). (15, 20) adds 5, the rule, instead of the relationship.

items.q: Ordered pairs are written (Pattern A term, Pattern B term). Where does the first number come from?
items.e: The first number is a term of Pattern A and the second number is the term in the same place in Pattern B.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. Which ordered pair (A term, B term) will be in the list?
items.e: Each B term is 3 times the A term, so 20 goes with 20 × 3 = 60: (20, 60). (20, 24) adds 4, and (24, 60) pairs the 7th term of A with the 6th term of B.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 6. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 30. The ordered pair (30, ?) is in the list. What is the missing number?
items.e: 30 is the 6th term of A. The 6th term of B is 5 × 30 = 150, because 30 = 5 × 6. (180 is the 7th term of B: one jump too many.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 125. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 500. In one ordered pair (A term, B term), the first number is 1,000. What is the second number?
items.e: 500 = 4 × 125, so each B term is 4 times the A term: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000. (4,500 is the next B term: one jump too many.)

items.q: Pattern A: start at 1, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 4, Add 1. The pairs start (1, 4), (2, 5), (3, 6). What is the 5th ordered pair?
items.e: The 5th terms are 1 + 4 = 5 and 4 + 4 = 8, so the pair is (5, 8). Each B term is 3 more than the A term. (5, 20) treats (1, 4) as “B is 4 times A,” but 2 × 4 is not 5.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 2, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 6, Add 6. Which list shows the first three ordered pairs (A term, B term)?
items.e: A: 2, 4, 6. B: 6, 12, 18. Pair the 1st terms, the 2nd terms and the 3rd terms, A first. The patterns start at 2 and 6, not 0.

items.q: Which graph shows the ordered pairs (A term, B term) from the table?
items.e: Graph 3. The pairs are (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4): go right by the A term and up by the B term. Graph 1 has x and y switched.

items.q: Which graph shows the ordered pairs (A term, B term) from the table?
items.e: Graph 4. The pairs are (0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4): each point is 1 higher than it is far right. Graph 1 has x and y switched.

items.q: Which graph shows the ordered pairs (A term, B term) from the table?
items.e: Graph 2. The pairs are (0, 1), (2, 2), (4, 3). Pattern A goes 0, 2, 4, so the points are 2 apart across. Graph 1 has x and y switched.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 2. Each point is (A term, B term). Which ordered pair does point P show?
items.e: Go down from P to the x-axis: 3. Go across from P to the y-axis: 6. So P is (3, 6), the 4th terms of A and B.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. Each point is (A term, B term). Which ordered pair does point P show?
items.e: Go down from P to the x-axis: 4. Go across from P to the y-axis: 12. So P is (4, 12), the 3rd terms of A and B. Read the numbers on the axes, not the number of grid spaces.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. Each point is (A term, B term). Which ordered pair does point P show?
items.e: Go down from P to the x-axis: 9. Go across from P to the y-axis: 18. So P is (9, 18), the 4th terms of A and B. Read the numbers on the axes, not the number of grid spaces.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 10. Each point is (A term, B term). Which ordered pair does point P show?
items.e: Go down from P to the x-axis: 10. Go across from P to the y-axis: 20. So P is (10, 20), the 3rd terms of A and B. Read the numbers on the axes, not the number of grid spaces.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 4. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 12. Each point is (A term, B term). Which ordered pair does point P show?
items.e: Go down from P to the x-axis: 12. Go across from P to the y-axis: 36. So P is (12, 36), the 4th terms of A and B. Read the numbers on the axes, not the number of grid spaces.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 2. The green points show the first 4 ordered pairs. Which red point shows the next ordered pair?
items.e: Point P. Pattern A adds 1 and Pattern B adds 2, so the next pair is (4, 8). (8, 4) has x and y switched, and (4, 7) adds 1 to the B term instead of 2.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 4. The green points show the first 4 ordered pairs. Which red point shows the next ordered pair?
items.e: Point P. Pattern A adds 2 and Pattern B adds 4, so the next pair is (8, 16). (16, 8) has x and y switched, and (10, 20) skips a pair: one jump too many.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 3. The green points show the first 3 ordered pairs. Which red point shows the next ordered pair?
items.e: Point R. Pattern A adds 1 and Pattern B adds 3, so the next pair is (3, 9). (9, 3) has x and y switched, and (2, 9) pairs the 3rd A term with the 4th B term.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 3, Add 1. The green points show the first 4 ordered pairs. Which red point shows the next ordered pair?
items.e: Point Q. Pattern A adds 1 and Pattern B adds 1, so the next pair is (4, 7). (7, 4) has x and y switched, and (5, 8) is one jump too many.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 2. Points P, Q, R and S should show the 2nd to 5th ordered pairs (A term, B term). Which point was plotted wrong?
items.e: Point S. It is at (8, 4), but the pair is (4, 8): x and y are switched.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 1. Points P, Q, R and S should show the 2nd to 5th ordered pairs (A term, B term). Which point was plotted wrong?
items.e: Point Q. It is at (4, 3), but the 3rd A term, 4, goes with the 3rd B term, 2. The point uses the next B term.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 1, Add 1. Pattern B: start at 3, Add 1. Points P, Q, R and S should show the 2nd to 5th ordered pairs (A term, B term). Which point was plotted wrong?
items.e: Point S. It is at (5, 8), but the 5th A term, 5, goes with the 5th B term, 7. The point uses the next B term.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 3. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 9. The ordered pairs (A term, B term) are graphed. Which point is also on the graph?
items.e: Each B term is 3 times the A term, so 15 goes with 45: (15, 45). (15, 24) adds 9 and (15, 18) adds 3 instead of using the relationship.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 6. The point (6, 18) is on the graph. How do you get from it to the next point?
items.e: The x-coordinate is the A term, which grows by 2. The y-coordinate is the B term, which grows by 6. So move right 2 and up 6, to (8, 24).

items.q: On a graph of (A term, B term), every point has a y-coordinate that is 4 times its x-coordinate. What does this tell you?
c: Each A term is 4 times the B term
Each B term is 4 more than the A term
Each B term is 4 times the A term
items.e: The x-coordinate is the A term and the y-coordinate is the B term. y = 4 × x means each B term is 4 times the corresponding A term.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 2. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 4. What do you notice about the graphed points?
c: They are on a straight line
They are all on the x-axis
They go down to the right
items.e: Each step goes right 2 and up 4, the same move every time, so the points line up in a straight line that starts at the origin.

items.q: Pattern A: start at 0, Add 5. Pattern B: start at 0, Add 15. The first graphed point is (0, 0). What does it show?
c: It is not a pair of terms
items.e: (0, 0) is the 1st ordered pair: the 1st term of A is 0 and the 1st term of B is 0.

sets.title: Word problems: two patterns in real life

items.q: Maya and Leo both start with $0. Each week Maya saves $3 and Leo saves $6. How much has Leo saved after 5 weeks?
items.e: Leo's pattern: $0, $6, $12, $18, $24, $30. After 5 weeks he has 5 × $6 = $30. ($36 is one week too many.)

items.q: Maya and Leo both start with $0. Each week Maya saves $3 and Leo saves $6. Which is true every week?
items.e: Week 1: $3 and $6. Week 2: $6 and $12. Week 3: $9 and $18. Leo always has 2 times as much, because he saves 2 times as much each week. The difference grows ($3, $6, $9), so “$3 more” is wrong.

items.q: Maya and Leo both start with $0. Each week Maya saves $3 and Leo saves $6. When Maya has $24, how much does Leo have?
items.e: Leo always has 2 times as much as Maya: 2 × $24 = $48. (Maya has $24 after 8 weeks, and 8 × $6 = $48.)

items.q: Maya and Leo both start with $0. Each week Maya saves $3 and Leo saves $6. The graph shows (Maya's savings, Leo's savings). What does point P mean?
items.e: P is at (9, 18). The x-axis is Maya's money and the y-axis is Leo's money, so when Maya has $9, Leo has $18 (after 3 weeks).

items.q: Maya and Leo both start with $0. Each week Maya saves $3 and Leo saves $6. The graph shows (Maya's savings, Leo's savings). Which ordered pair comes after (12, 24)?
items.e: Each week Maya's savings go up $3 and Leo's go up $6: (12 + 3, 24 + 6) = (15, 30). (15, 27) adds $3 to both.

items.q: A lemonade recipe uses 1 cup of lemon juice for every 4 cups of water. Lemon juice: 1, 2, 3, … cups. Water: 4, 8, 12, … cups. How many cups of water go with 5 cups of lemon juice?
items.e: The water pattern adds 4 and the juice pattern adds 1, so the water is always 4 times the juice: 5 × 4 = 20 cups. (5 + 4 = 9 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: A lemonade recipe uses 1 cup of lemon juice for every 4 cups of water. The ordered pairs are (cups of lemon juice, cups of water). Which ordered pair fits the recipe?
items.e: 3 cups of juice need 3 × 4 = 12 cups of water. Juice comes first: (3, 12). (3, 7) adds 4 instead.

items.q: Ava and Ben start hiking at the same time from the same place. Ava hikes 2 miles each hour and Ben hikes 4 miles each hour. How far has Ben hiked when Ava has hiked 7 miles?
items.e: Each hour Ben hikes 2 times as far as Ava, and both start at 0, so Ben's distance is always 2 times Ava's: 2 × 7 = 14 miles.

items.q: Ava and Ben start hiking at the same time from the same place. Ava hikes 2 miles each hour and Ben hikes 4 miles each hour. Why is Ben's distance always 2 times Ava's distance?
c: They hike for the same time
items.e: Every hour Ben adds 4 miles and Ava adds 2 miles. 4 = 2 × 2, so after any number of hours Ben has added 2 times as much. Because both started at 0, Ben's total is always 2 times Ava's.

items.q: For a fundraiser, Class A raises $150 each week and Class B raises $450 each week. Both start at $0. How much has Class B raised after 8 weeks?
items.e: Class B adds $450 each week: 8 × $450 = $3,600. It is also 3 times Class A's $1,200. ($4,050 is one week too many.)

items.q: Two empty tanks are filled with water. Tank A gets 25 liters each minute and tank B gets 100 liters each minute. When tank A has 500 liters, how much does tank B have?
items.e: 100 = 4 × 25, and both start empty, so tank B always has 4 times as much: 500 × 4 = 2,000 liters.

items.q: Zoe is 8 years old and her brother is 5. Each year, both get 1 year older. How old will Zoe be when her brother is 12?
items.e: Zoe is 3 years older (8 − 5 = 3), and both add 1 each year, so she stays 3 years older: 12 + 3 = 15. (12 × 3 = 36 treats it as times.)

items.q: Zoe is 8 years old and her brother is 5. Why will Zoe always be 3 years older than her brother?
c: Both get 1 year older each year
Zoe gets 3 years older each year
Zoe's age is 3 times his age
items.e: The difference starts at 8 − 5 = 3. Each year both ages add the same number, 1, so the difference stays 3: 8 and 5, 9 and 6, 10 and 7.

items.q: Nora swims 2 laps each day and Sam swims 6 laps each day. They start on the same day. When Sam has swum 42 laps in all, how many laps has Nora swum?
items.e: 6 = 3 × 2, so Sam's total is always 3 times Nora's. Work backward: 42 ÷ 3 = 14 laps. (Both have swum for 7 days: 7 × 2 = 14.)

items.q: A motorcycle has 2 wheels and a car has 4 wheels. The ordered pairs are (wheels on the motorcycles, wheels on the cars) for the same number of each. Which ordered pair is for 7 motorcycles and 7 cars?
items.e: 7 motorcycles have 7 × 2 = 14 wheels and 7 cars have 7 × 4 = 28 wheels: (14, 28). (7, 28) uses the number of motorcycles, not their wheels, and (2, 4) is for only 1 of each.

items.q: Maya's pattern starts at 0 and adds 4. Leo wants each term of his pattern to be 3 times the matching term of Maya's. His pattern also starts at 0. Which rule should he use?
items.e: Each step Leo must add 3 times as much as Maya: 3 × 4 = 12. Check: 4 and 12, 8 and 24, 12 and 36. (Add 7 is 4 + 3.)

items.q: Ruby's Pattern A starts at 2 and adds 6. She wants each term of Pattern B to be 5 more than the matching A term. Which start and rule should Pattern B have?
items.e: To stay 5 more, B must start 5 higher (2 + 5 = 7) and grow by the same amount, 6. Adding 11 each time would make the difference grow: 7 and 2, 18 and 8.

items.q: Printer A prints 120 pages each minute and printer B prints 480 pages each minute. They start at the same time. When printer A has printed 1,080 pages, how many has printer B printed?
items.e: 480 = 4 × 120, so printer B always prints 4 times as many pages: 1,080 × 4 = 4,320 pages.

items.q: Ava reads 10 pages each day and Eli reads 30 pages each day, starting on the same day. Ava says Eli has always read 20 more pages than she has. Is she right?
c: No, he has read 3 times as many
No, he has read 20 times as many
items.e: Day 1: 10 and 30 (20 more). Day 2: 20 and 60 (40 more). The difference grows, but Eli's total is always 3 times Ava's, because 30 = 3 × 10.

items.q: A pancake recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 1 cup of milk. The ordered pairs (cups of milk, cups of flour) are graphed. Which point is not on the graph?
items.e: The flour is always 2 times the milk, and milk comes first. (8, 4) has the numbers switched: 8 cups of milk would need 16 cups of flour.
